document.title: Discussing Afghan Policy with the Pakistanis (State 291940)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] State questions Pakistan's policy of backing any group opposed to the Rabbani government, including the Taliban. It doubts Pakistan can control the Taliban ('falls short of being able to call the shots') and notes Tehran, Moscow and New Delhi wrongly assume the U.S. shares Pakistan's support for the Taliban.

persons.name: Burhanuddin Rabbani
persons.role: Nominal head of the Kabul government (President of Afghanistan)

mentions.quote: THE GOP APPEARS AMBIVALENT, AT BEST, ABOUT WHETHER RABBANI AND MASOOD SHOULD HAVE ANY PLACE IN TRANSITIONAL ARRANGEMENTS
THE GOP ADOPTED A MORE OPENLY ANTI-RABBANI STANCE IN 1995

persons.name: Ahmad Shah Masood
persons.role: Rabbani's military ally; Kabul regime defense figure with forces in the Panjshir

mentions.quote: A/S RAPHEL'S MEETING WITH MASOOD ON OCTOBER 30, THE KABUL AUTHORITIES CLEARLY FEEL ALIENATED FROM THE U.S.
HIS TROOPS RETREATING TO THE PANJSHIR TO RETURN AND FIGHT

persons.name: Ismael Khan

mentions.quote: THE FORCES OF RABBANI ALLY ISMAEL KHAN PUSHED THE TALIBAN TO GIRISHK NEAR THEIR HOME BASE AT KANDAHAR

persons.name: Abdul Rashid Dostam
persons.role: Northern faction leader courted by Pakistan for an anti-Rabbani alliance

mentions.quote: DOSTAM WAS NOT OPTIMISTIC DURING HIS EARLY NOVEMBER MEETING WITH A/S RAPHEL

persons.name: Gulbuddin Hekmatyar
persons.role: Faction leader; Pakistan sought alliance with him; possibly cooperating with Kabul

events.description: The Taliban and Wahdat were thrown back from Kabul.
Forces of Ismael Khan pushed the Taliban back to Girishk.
Taliban rolled up Ismael Khan's troops, took Shindand airbase and entered Herat without a battle, covering about 450 km in 5 days.
Mob attack on the Pakistani embassy and personnel in Kabul after the fall of Herat, which the cable says could not have occurred without regime involvement.
A/S Raphel met Masood.
A/S Raphel visited Moscow; Russian support for Rabbani had hardened.
Dostam met A/S Raphel in early November.
FonMin Assef Ali held a press conference criticizing Mestiri's plan.
A/S Raphel discussed Afghan policy with Pakistani PermRep Kamal.
State Department cable to Embassy Islamabad with talking points on Afghan policy.
Taliban and Wahdat were thrown back from Kabul, leaving Kabul free of fighting for the first time in three years.
By late August Ismael Khan's forces pushed the Taliban back to Girishk near Kandahar.
Taliban routed Ismael Khan's troops, took Shindand airbase and entered Herat without a battle, covering about 450 km in 5 days.
Ismael Khan fled to Iran after the fall of Herat.
Mob attack on the Pakistani embassy and personnel in Kabul after the fall of Herat, which the cable says could not have happened without active regime involvement.
Assistant Secretary Raphel visited Moscow and found Russian support for Rabbani had hardened.
State Department cable instructing Embassy Islamabad to discuss Afghan policy with Pakistani policymakers.
Assef Ali told US officials Pakistan would try to unite all parties opposing Rabbani.
Pakistan adopts openly anti-Rabbani stance.
Mob attack on Pakistani Embassy and personnel in Kabul following the fall of Herat.
Dostam met A/S Raphel.
Raphel met Masood.
Assef Ali press conference criticizing Mestiri's plan.
Raphel discussion with Pakistan Permrep Kamal.
State Department cable sent with talking points for Pakistan.

key_claims: Pakistan has followed a policy of supporting the Taliban and trying to forge a military and political alliance among Kabul's opponents.
Pakistan's 'Rabbani must go at any price' policy, including a Taliban takeover of Kabul, hardened Russian, Iranian and Indian support for Rabbani.
The U.S. doubts Pakistan can control the Taliban; it has some influence but cannot call the shots.
The Taliban's capture of Herat and flight of Ismael Khan to Iran intensified Iranian fear of the Taliban and led Tehran to back Kabul.
The U.S. doubts a Taliban victory would produce a stable, representative government and expects an unrepresentative Pashtun authority to replace an unrepresentative Tajik regime.
Tehran, Moscow and New Delhi wrongly assume the U.S. is party to Pakistan's support for the Taliban, which undermines U.S. credibility and support for the UN mission.
